podcast.body: Despite becoming a Christmas favorite, the song is not traditionally Christmassy, focusing instead on a fight between a drunken couple on Christmas Eve. It took over two years to write and record, starting as a piece by banjo player Jim Finer in 1985. "Not very Christmassy in the traditional sense, but still one of the biggest alt rock Christmas songs ever, if not of all time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inspiration and Concept Shift
podcast.body: Returning to England in March 1986, the song's concept changed from a sailor to a drunken couple's Christmas Eve fight. Part of the inspiration came from a book Shane McGowan read on tour, "A Fairy Tale of New York," about an Irish man returning to New York after studying in Ireland. "Part of the inspiration came from a book that Shane had read on tour called A Fairy Tale of New York, which dealt with an Irish dude returning to New York after going to school in Ireland."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Long Development
podcast.body: Jim Finer first started developing the song in 1985, showing it to Shane McGowan. For the next two years, they struggled with the lyrics, which initially centered on a lonely sailor, a concept deemed "crap." The band blew off recording it for Christmas 1985 and went on tour in America. "It first started to come together as a piece sometime in 1985 by Jim Feiner, the Pogs Banjo player."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Separate Vocal Recordings
podcast.body: A notable curiosity of "Fairy Tale of New York" is that, despite being a duet, Shane McGowan and Kirsty MacColl never recorded their parts together in the same studio. MacColl recorded her vocals separately based on Shane's demo, and then Shane adjusted his vocals. "As you listen to this, remember that although the song was written as a duet and sung as a duet, Shane and Kirsty were never ever in the same studio together."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vocalist Challenges
podcast.body: The Pogues faced difficulty finding a suitable female vocalist for the duet. It was initially written for bass player Cait O'Riordan, but she left the band after running off with Elvis Costello, shelving the song for Christmas 1986. "Besides, the Pogs really couldn't find anybody they liked to sing the female part."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
